\chapter{See You Soon}
\label{ch:la-see-you-soon}
\hlchaptermodality{24}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can tell someone in Latin that I will see them soon, using a phrase Cicero actually wrote.}

Say propediem tē vidēbō as a parting line, split propediem into prope and diem, and locate it in Cicero's letters.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[propediem tē vidēbō]{propediem tē vidēbō — a real change of pace: solidly attested, twice}

\label{lesson:LA-C24-propediem-te-videbo}



\begin{quote}
The last few lessons were honest about real gaps — no fixed \textquotedblleft{}how are you,\textquotedblright{} no fixed \textquotedblleft{}nice to meet you,\textquotedblright{} no fixed \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} This one is different: a genuine, repeated Ciceronian phrase.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: propediem tē vidēbō — \textquotedblleft{}I shall see you soon\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Propediem tē vidēbō} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I shall see you soon}\textquotedblright{} — is genuinely attested, not once but \textbf{twice}, in \textbf{Cicero}'s own letters:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Ad Familiārēs 2.12} (to Caelius): \emph{\textquotedblleft{}Sed, ut spērō, propediem tē vidēbō\textquotedblright{}} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{But, as I hope, I shall see you soon.}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{Ad Familiārēs 15.6} (to Cato): \emph{\textquotedblleft{}Ego, ut spērō, tē propediem vidēbō\textquotedblright{}} — the same phrase, word order reshuffled, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I, as I hope, shall see you soon.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Propediem} breaks down as \textbf{prope} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{near}\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{diem} (accusative of \textbf{diēs}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{near the day},\textquotedblright{} meaning \textquotedblleft{}very soon, shortly.\textquotedblright{} That's the \textbf{same diēs} from your days-of-week lessons (\emph{diēs Lūnae}, \emph{diēs Veneris}) — a familiar root showing up in a brand-new job.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: vidēbō — the verb ending doing the work, again}]
\textbf{Vidēbō} is the \textbf{future tense} of \textbf{vidēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} — and just like \emph{agō} back in \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} the \textbf{-bō} ending already carries \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I will},\textquotedblright{} so no separate pronoun for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} is needed. \emph{Tē} (\textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) is simply the direct object: \textquotedblleft{}{[}I{]} will-see you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}propediem tē vidēbō\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}I shall see you soon\textquotedblright{}
  \item propediem's own pieces — prope (near) + diem (the day)
  \item the honest contrast — unlike the last few lessons, this phrase IS solidly attested, twice, in Cicero
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where is \textbf{propediem tē vidēbō} genuinely attested, and how many times? (\textbf{Twice}, in \textbf{Cicero}'s letters — \emph{Ad Familiārēs} 2.12 and 15.6.) What does \textbf{propediem} literally break down into? (\textbf{Prope} \textquotedblleft{}near\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{diem} \textquotedblleft{}the day\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{diēs} from the days-of-week lessons.) Does \emph{vidēbō} need a separate word for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — the \emph{-bō} future ending already carries it, the same way \emph{agō}'s \emph{-ō} did.)
\end{tcolorbox}
